newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitians show little enthusiam in local elections.
newsitem.headline: Haitians show little enthusiam in local elections.

text.p: Only a handful of Haitians turned up to vote on Sunday morning in senate and local elections, with many staying away in protest against government privatisation plans and worsening poverty.
Although people gathered outside polling stations in the capital Port-au-Prince, many said they were disillusioned with politicians and did not plan to cast a ballot.

"We are hungry. We can't vote for millionaires. The senators got millions from the Americans and what did we get? Nothing. If they pay us we'll vote," said one man outside the Alexandre Petain school in downtown Port-au-Prince as a crowd shouted in agreement.

The polls are the fifth electoral exercise in Haiti since a U.S. military intervention ousted a military regime and restored the popular president Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power in October 1994. Rene Preval was elected as his successor in December 1995.

But Preval's plans to ease poverty through a privatisation progam backed with huge infusions of international aid have stalled and people are growing even more hungry and desperate in a country that is already the poorest in the Western hemisphere.

At the school polling station, election officials outnumbered voters. Chief supervisor Lebrun Ruoat said only one person turned up to cast a ballot in the first few hours of voting although more people might come after Sunday mass.

"The country is in a bad situation. They voted for candidates and when they came into power candidates voted for privatisation laws. We are in a situation where people don't believe anymore," he said.

At another polling place, the first person to turn up was unable to find his name on the voters' list. Although police had promised a heavy presence to ensure security, not one officer was to be seen at the Alexander Petain school.
At stake in the polls are nine seats in the 27-seat Senate, two parliamentary seats, 133 town delegations and 565 district assemblies. More than four million Haitians are registered to vote.

The election aims to bring democratic rule to a local level for the first time in the history of the Caribbean state, which achieved independence with a slave revolt in 1804 but has since suffered a tortured history of rule by dictators and generals with occassional military interventions by the United States.

Foreign analysts say the poll will signal what the future may hold for Haiti. The ruling Lavalas Political Organisation has already split over privatisation. Aristide founded the Famni Lavalas (Lavalas Family) in November and it is fielding slates of candidates against former colleagues.
Senator Yvon Neptune said Famnia Lavalas stood for the orginal Lavalas' ideals and carried the banner of the party of the poor.

"Famni Lavalas is for economic reform but with the participation of the people. Famni Lavalas is against the exploitation of the Haitian people and against decisions supposedly taken in their name but without them having a say in it," he said, referring to the international community's plans for Haiti.

The elections take place against a background of increased violence in which more than 50 people have been killed in the past two months. Although the bloodshed seems largely criminal rather than political, it has heightened the mood of fear and misery. Nonetheless a United Nations peacekeeping force is due to pull out when its mandate expires at the end of July.
